title: Determinants of Electric Vehicle Adoption in Malaysia with the Moderating Role of Government Incentives
content: This study investigates the key determinants of Electric Vehicle Adoption in Malaysia by integrating technological, environmental, and safety related perceptions together with the moderating role of government incentives. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Theory of Planned Behaviour, and Diffusion of Innovation Theory, the study examines how perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived green value, and perceived safety influence adoption intention. A quantitative approach was employed using data from 124 Malaysian respondents and analysed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling. The results show that all four predictors significantly and positively influence Electric Vehicle Adoption, with perceived usefulness emerging as the strongest driver, followed by perceived ease of use and perceived safety. Perceived green value also demonstrates a positive effect, although comparatively weaker. The Importance Performance Map Analysis further highlights usefulness, ease of use, and safety as the most influential levers for improving adoption outcomes. Moderation analysis reveals that government incentives strengthen the effects of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, indicating that financial and policy support amplify the practical and functional value associated with electric vehicles. However, incentives do not influence the effects of perceived green value or perceived safety, suggesting that environmental and safety evaluations are formed independently of policy interventions. The findings provide meaningful insights for policymakers, manufacturers, and industry stakeholders to strengthen incentive structures, enhance user convenience, and communicate performance benefits to accelerate electric vehicle adoption in Malaysia.
